outline.keyPoint: Many parents are surprised that their eleven-year-old already has informatics. At a Bavarian Gymnasium it sits inside the science subject «Natur und Technik», and it does not start with coding. It starts with order: how do you describe the things inside a computer, and how are they arranged? This video is for parents who do not speak German. You learn what the curriculum expects, which pictures carry the ideas, the German words your child will use, and how to practise at the computer at home without needing any German.

In the Bavarian curriculum, the «LehrplanPLUS», the subject «Natur und Technik» in Year six has an informatics part alongside the science part. The informatics part has three topics. The first, by far the biggest with about eighteen lessons, is about representing information as text, images, diagrams and sound, and introduces objects, attributes, methods and classes. The second is a project, a multimedia presentation. The third, the subject of this video, is called «Hierarchische Informationsstrukturen», hierarchical information structures, with the file system as the example. It is short, about five lessons, but it introduces the tree, one of the most important structures in informatics.

The curriculum lists the content precisely. First, the two classes «DATEI», file, and «ORDNER», folder, with their recursive contains relationship: a folder contains files, but also folders. Second, the tree with its terms «Wurzel», «Knoten», «Kante» and «Blatt», that is root, node, edge and leaf. Third, the path, «der Pfad», which locates a file in the tree without ambiguity. Your child should recognise this structure, name it and use it, for example by creating sensible folders and reading paths. Which tasks are practised and tested is the teacher's decision.

Four pictures carry the topic, and all four show the same example computer: the folder of a girl called Mia with school, photos and music. First the tree with its vocabulary, then the path as a route through the tree, then the two classes behind it, and finally a small piece of statistics that makes the recursive idea practical: how big is a folder? The captions on screen are German, exactly as your child sees them in class.

Idea one: the tree, «der Baum». The top folder is the root, «die Wurzel». Every folder and every file is a node, «ein Knoten». The lines are edges, «Kanten», and each one means contains. Nodes without children, that is the files, are leaves, «Blätter». The words come from real trees, except that this one grows downwards, with the root at the top, which confuses children at first. A file cannot contain anything, so files are always leaves; an empty folder is a leaf too.

Idea two: the path, «der Pfad». It describes the way from the root to a file, folder by folder, separated by slashes: Mia, «Fotos», «Urlaub», strand dot j p g, a photo of the beach. «Fotos» is photos, «Urlaub» is holiday. On Windows the backslash appears instead; the meaning is the same. What matters is uniqueness: two files may share a name if they sit in different folders, because their paths differ. This is why the school model is a tree and not a web: every file has exactly one parent folder, so exactly one way leads from the root to it.

Idea three: the classes. Bavarian school informatics describes the world in an object-oriented way from the very start. The class «ORDNER» has the attribute «name». The class «DATEI» has «name» and «größe», size. The relationship «enthält», contains, is drawn as an arrow. Every actual folder and file is an object of its class, written in lower case: the object «aufsatz» of class «DATEI» has the name Aufsatz dot t x t, in dot notation «aufsatz Punkt name». The arrow from folder to file means contains; «enthält» is a relationship drawn as an arrow, not an attribute. The arrow from folder back to folder is the recursive link, «rekursiv»: a folder contains folders. That one word explains why a tree can grow as deep as you like.

Idea four: a little statistics. In this model only files have a size; a folder's size is the sum of all files inside it, down to the leaves. «Schule», school, ten megabytes; «Fotos», photos, seventeen, the biggest bar and therefore highlighted; «Musik», music, fifteen. As a bar chart, «Säulendiagramm», the comparison is visible at a glance, and this links the topic to the first informatics topic: the same information shown as a list, as a tree or as a chart. And the calculation itself is recursive again: a folder's size needs the sizes of its subfolders.

Here are the words in one place, in three groups: the words for the tree, the words for classes and objects, which matter far beyond this topic, and a few everyday computer words that differ from English. Good news first: many of the terms are the same Latin or Greek words as in English, so you will recognise «Objekt», «Klasse», «Attribut» and «rekursiv» straight away. The tree words are plain German and worth learning.

A file is «die Datei», plural «die Dateien»; a folder is «der Ordner», unchanged in the plural; the whole arrangement is «das Dateisystem». The tree is «der Baum», its root «die Wurzel», a node «der Knoten», plural «die Knoten». An edge is «die Kante», a leaf «das Blatt», plural «die Blätter». The path is «der Pfad». The file extension, the part after the dot, is «die Dateiendung». One trap: «Ordner» in everyday German also means a ring binder, the thing with paper in it, much like the English word folder, which also comes from paper filing.

The class is «die Klasse», written in capitals in Bavarian schoolbooks: «ORDNER», «DATEI». An object is «das Objekt», one concrete folder or file, written in lower case. An attribute is «das Attribut»: «name», or «größe», which means size. Dot notation is «die Punktnotation»: object dot attribute, as in «aufsatz Punkt name». The link between classes is «die Beziehung», relationship, and when it points back to the same class it is «rekursiv». These words come back in later informatics lessons, though how far depends on the school and the course your child chooses.

A quick check for you. Your child points at the picture and says: «Der Ordner Urlaub ist kein Blatt». The folder «Urlaub», holiday, is not a leaf. Is that right, and why? Take a moment. Remember the definition: a leaf is a node without children. What hangs below the holiday folder?

Your child is right. The folder «Urlaub» contains three photo files, so it has children, and a node with children is an inner node, not a leaf. The three photos themselves are leaves, because nothing hangs below them. This is the kind of reasoning the topic asks for: not memorising that files are leaves, but checking the definition. If you want to test it further, ask about an empty folder: it has no children, so by the definition it is a leaf as well.

This topic is easier to practise at home than almost any other, because the material is on the desk: your child's computer, tablet or phone. Three exercises of about ten minutes each train exactly what the curriculum asks, and tidy the device as a side effect. You need no informatics and no German; your child explains the tree and supplies the words, and you ask the questions.

Exercise one: your child draws their own school folder as a tree on paper, root at the top, files as leaves at the bottom, and labels it with the German words «Wurzel», «Knoten», «Kante», «Blatt». You ask: which nodes are leaves, and how do you know? Is there an empty folder, and is that a leaf? The drawing usually reveals that the real folder is a mess, which leads straight to exercise three.

Exercise two: paths. The file manager shows the path of an open file in its address bar. Your child reads it aloud: root, folder, subfolder, file. Then the other way round: you write a path, your child finds the file. Most instructive are two files with the same name in different folders; they make the uniqueness of paths tangible. The slash and backslash question settles itself here without theory. On a phone the tree is hidden, so a computer is better for this exercise.

Exercise three: show the sizes of the top folders, on a computer via properties or get info, and sketch a bar chart together. Ask: why is this folder so big, which files inside make it so? That is the recursive idea in practice. Then tidy up: create sensible folders, give files meaningful names, delete duplicates. A child who organises their own tree is well on the way to understanding the topic, and finds their homework again as a bonus.

Three things parents often ask. Which wrong ideas are common? How is the informatics part of «Natur und Technik» assessed? And how does informatics continue at the Gymnasium? The misconceptions mostly come from everyday language and from devices that hide the tree. The assessment is lighter than in the main subjects. And informatics stays with your child for years.

Four misconceptions from many classes. One: a folder stores content itself. No, it only contains; in the school model only files carry information and size, and the computer shows a folder's size as the sum of its files. Two: the tree grows upwards like a real one. In informatics the root is at the top. Three: leaf is just another word for file. Almost, but the definition is a node without children, and an empty folder counts. Four, the most stubborn: with a search box nobody needs structure. Phones hide the tree, but it is there, and a child who understands paths finds files even when search fails.

In Year six, «Natur und Technik» is usually one of the subjects without the big written tests called «Schulaufgaben». Grades usually come from smaller pieces: short unannounced tests, «Stegreifaufgaben», oral participation, practical work at the computer, and in the informatics part often the presentation project from the second topic. Possible tasks on the file system include: label a tree with the four terms, give the path of a file or find a file from its path, read a class diagram, assign objects to their class. How exactly your child's school handles this is the teacher's decision.

How does it continue? In the following years informatics usually continues, first inside «Natur und Technik» and later in lessons of its own; the exact timetable depends on the school and the branch of the Gymnasium, so check the school's own information. The way of thinking from Year six carries on: objects, classes, attributes and relationships are the foundation for everything that follows. And the tree keeps coming back, in document outlines, menus, databases and the structure of web pages. What your child learns now at the file system is a basic pattern of the whole discipline, not a side topic.

In short: the informatics part of «Natur und Technik» teaches a way of thinking. Describe things as objects with a class and attributes, see structures as a tree with root, nodes, edges and leaves, give locations as a unique path, and understand the recursive idea that folders contain folders. Practise at your child's own computer: draw the tree, read paths, compare sizes, tidy up, and let your child supply the German words. In this model only files have a size; a folder's size is the sum of all files inside it, down to the leaves. «Schule», school, ten megabytes; «Fotos», photos, seventeen, the biggest bar and therefore highlighted; «Musik», music, fifteen. As a bar chart, «Säulendiagramm», the comparison is visible at a glance, and this links the topic to the first informatics topic: the same information shown as a list, as a tree or as a chart. And the calculation itself is recursive again: a folder's size needs the sizes of its subfolders.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Idea 4: folder sizes as a chart

scenes.narration: Here are the words in one place, in three groups: the words for the tree, the words for classes and objects, which matter far beyond this topic, and a few everyday computer words that differ from English. Good news first: many of the terms are the same Latin or Greek words as in English, so you will recognise «Objekt», «Klasse», «Attribut» and «rekursiv» straight away. The tree words are plain German and worth learning.
scenes.onScreenTitle: The words your child brings home

scenes.narration: A file is «die Datei», plural «die Dateien»; a folder is «der Ordner», unchanged in the plural; the whole arrangement is «das Dateisystem». The tree is «der Baum», its root «die Wurzel», a node «der Knoten», plural «die Knoten». An edge is «die Kante», a leaf «das Blatt», plural «die Blätter». The path is «der Pfad». The file extension, the part after the dot, is «die Dateiendung». One trap: «Ordner» in everyday German also means a ring binder, the thing with paper in it, much like the English word folder, which also comes from paper filing.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Tree words

scenes.narration: The class is «die Klasse», written in capitals in Bavarian schoolbooks: «ORDNER», «DATEI». An object is «das Objekt», one concrete folder or file, written in lower case. An attribute is «das Attribut»: «name», or «größe», which means size. Dot notation is «die Punktnotation»: object dot attribute, as in «aufsatz Punkt name». The link between classes is «die Beziehung», relationship, and when it points back to the same class it is «rekursiv». These words come back in later informatics lessons, though how far depends on the school and the course your child chooses.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Class and object words

scenes.narration: A quick check for you. Your child points at the picture and says: «Der Ordner Urlaub ist kein Blatt». The folder «Urlaub», holiday, is not a leaf. Is that right, and why? Take a moment. Remember the definition: a leaf is a node without children. What hangs below the holiday folder?
scenes.onScreenTitle: The words your child brings home

scenes.narration: Your child is right. The folder «Urlaub» contains three photo files, so it has children, and a node with children is an inner node, not a leaf. The three photos themselves are leaves, because nothing hangs below them. This is the kind of reasoning the topic asks for: not memorising that files are leaves, but checking the definition. If you want to test it further, ask about an empty folder: it has no children, so by the definition it is a leaf as well.
scenes.onScreenTitle: The answer

scenes.narration: This topic is easier to practise at home than almost any other, because the material is on the desk: your child's computer, tablet or phone. Three exercises of about ten minutes each train exactly what the curriculum asks, and tidy the device as a side effect. You need no informatics and no German; your child explains the tree and supplies the words, and you ask the questions.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Practising at the computer at home

scenes.narration: Exercise one: your child draws their own school folder as a tree on paper, root at the top, files as leaves at the bottom, and labels it with the German words «Wurzel», «Knoten», «Kante», «Blatt». You ask: which nodes are leaves, and how do you know? Is there an empty folder, and is that a leaf? The drawing usually reveals that the real folder is a mess, which leads straight to exercise three.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Exercise 1: draw your own tree

scenes.narration: Exercise two: paths. The file manager shows the path of an open file in its address bar. Your child reads it aloud: root, folder, subfolder, file. Then the other way round: you write a path, your child finds the file. Most instructive are two files with the same name in different folders; they make the uniqueness of paths tangible. The slash and backslash question settles itself here without theory. On a phone the tree is hidden, so a computer is better for this exercise.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Exercise 2: read and write paths

scenes.narration: Exercise three: show the sizes of the top folders, on a computer via properties or get info, and sketch a bar chart together. Ask: why is this folder so big, which files inside make it so? That is the recursive idea in practice. Then tidy up: create sensible folders, give files meaningful names, delete duplicates. A child who organises their own tree is well on the way to understanding the topic, and finds their homework again as a bonus.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Exercise 3: compare sizes and tidy up

scenes.narration: Three things parents often ask. Which wrong ideas are common? How is the informatics part of «Natur und Technik» assessed? And how does informatics continue at the Gymnasium? The misconceptions mostly come from everyday language and from devices that hide the tree. The assessment is lighter than in the main subjects. And informatics stays with your child for years.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Misconceptions, assessment, and what comes next

scenes.narration: Four misconceptions from many classes. One: a folder stores content itself. No, it only contains; in the school model only files carry information and size, and the computer shows a folder's size as the sum of its files. Two: the tree grows upwards like a real one. In informatics the root is at the top. Three: leaf is just another word for file. Almost, but the definition is a node without children, and an empty folder counts. Four, the most stubborn: with a search box nobody needs structure. Phones hide the tree, but it is there, and a child who understands paths finds files even when search fails.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Four common misconceptions

scenes.narration: In Year six, «Natur und Technik» is usually one of the subjects without the big written tests called «Schulaufgaben». Grades usually come from smaller pieces: short unannounced tests, «Stegreifaufgaben», oral participation, practical work at the computer, and in the informatics part often the presentation project from the second topic. Possible tasks on the file system include: label a tree with the four terms, give the path of a file or find a file from its path, read a class diagram, assign objects to their class. How exactly your child's school handles this is the teacher's decision.
scenes.onScreenTitle: How this subject is usually assessed

scenes.narration: How does it continue? In the following years informatics usually continues, first inside «Natur und Technik» and later in lessons of its own; the exact timetable depends on the school and the branch of the Gymnasium, so check the school's own information. The way of thinking from Year six carries on: objects, classes, attributes and relationships are the foundation for everything that follows. And the tree keeps coming back, in document outlines, menus, databases and the structure of web pages. What your child learns now at the file system is a basic pattern of the whole discipline, not a side topic.
scenes.onScreenTitle: What comes next: informatics stays

scenes.narration: In short: the informatics part of «Natur und Technik» teaches a way of thinking. Describe things as objects with a class and attributes, see structures as a tree with root, nodes, edges and leaves, give locations as a unique path, and understand the recursive idea that folders contain folders. Practise at your child's own computer: draw the tree, read paths, compare sizes, tidy up, and let your child supply the German words. The German version of this guide and the lesson for children are on this channel. Subscribe for the next topic.

publish.description:
Your eleven-year-old already has informatics inside the subject Natur und Technik. It starts with order, not coding: classes, objects, attributes and a tree every child knows from the computer. This guide explains the topic, the German terms, and three exercises at the computer at home.

In this video:
• Where informatics sits in Year 6 and what topic NT6 2.3 expects
• The core ideas in 3D pictures: tree, path, the classes DATEI and ORDNER, recursion, folder sizes as a chart
• German terms: Datei, Ordner, Wurzel, Knoten, Kante, Blatt, Pfad, Klasse, Objekt, Attribut, rekursiv
• Three exercises at home without any German
• Common misconceptions and how the subject is assessed

For whom: international parents of Year 6 pupils (Jahrgangsstufe 6) at a Gymnasium in Bavaria.

Curriculum: LehrplanPLUS Gymnasium Bayern, Natur und Technik 6, Lernbereich NT6 2.3 Hierarchische Informationsstrukturen, Dateisystem.
